A_target.statement:
Let $\mathbf A$ be a real $m \times n$ [[Definition:Matrix|matrix]].
Then there exist [[Definition:Orthogonal Matrix|orthogonal matrices]] $\mathbf U$, $\mathbf V$ and a [[Definition:Diagonal Matrix|diagonal]] $\mathbf \Sigma$ with non-negative entries such that:
:$\mathbf A = \mathbf U \mathbf \Sigma \mathbf V^\intercal$

B_source.statement:
Let $\mathbf M$ be a real [[Definition:Symmetric Matrix|symmetric matrix]].
Then $\mathbf M = \mathbf Q \mathbf D \mathbf Q^\intercal$ with $\mathbf Q$ orthogonal and $\mathbf D$ real diagonal.

substitutions.eigenvectors of M (columns of Q): the right singular vectors (columns of V)

object_map.reformulation: Apply the spectral theorem to the symmetric positive-semidefinite matrix A^T A, then recover U from the relation A = U S V^T.

validity_conditions: A^T A is symmetric and positive semidefinite, so the spectral theorem gives A^T A = V S^2 V^T with S^2 >= 0.
Singular values s_i = sqrt(eigenvalue_i) are real and nonnegative.
For nonzero singular values, u_i = A v_i / s_i are orthonormal and extend to an orthogonal U, giving A = U S V^T.
proof_plan: Form $\mathbf A^\intercal \mathbf A$, which is symmetric, and [[Definition:Positive Semidefinite Matrix|positive semidefinite]] as $\mathbf x^\intercal \mathbf A^\intercal \mathbf A \mathbf x = \norm {\mathbf A \mathbf x}^2 \ge 0$.

By the [[Spectral Theorem for Real Symmetric Matrices|spectral theorem]]:
:$\mathbf A^\intercal \mathbf A = \mathbf V \mathbf \Sigma^2 \mathbf V^\intercal$
with orthonormal eigenvectors $\mathbf v_i$ and eigenvalues $\sigma_i^2 \ge 0$.

Let $\sigma_i = \sqrt {\sigma_i^2}$, and for $\sigma_i > 0$ let $\mathbf u_i = \dfrac {\mathbf A \mathbf v_i} {\sigma_i}$.
Then $\innerprod {\mathbf u_i} {\mathbf u_j} = \dfrac {\mathbf v_i^\intercal \mathbf A^\intercal \mathbf A \mathbf v_j} {\sigma_i \sigma_j} = \delta_{i j}$, and extend to an orthonormal basis.

Then $\mathbf A \mathbf v_i = \sigma_i \mathbf u_i$ for all $i$, so $\mathbf A \mathbf V = \mathbf U \mathbf \Sigma$ and:
:$\mathbf A = \mathbf U \mathbf \Sigma \mathbf V^\intercal$
which is the [[Singular Value Decomposition]].
{{qed}}
